en.title: Education Chemistry: the whole course
en.short: What education chemistry covers, how the degree is organised, the main areas and how to study them.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text: Education Chemistry is a teacher-education degree that joins the subject of chemistry with the study of teaching. About half of the work is chemistry: matter, reactions, calculations, bonding, analysis and laboratory practice. The other half is education: how learners think, how a curriculum is built, how to teach chemistry, how to assess learning, how to manage a class and how to conduct teaching practice. The aim is a graduate who understands chemistry deeply and can explain it safely and clearly. Graduates may teach in schools, work in laboratories, help develop curriculum materials or continue to research chemistry education.

sections.heading: How the degree is usually organised
sections.text: Degree length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria, universities commonly offer B.Sc.(Ed) or B.Ed programmes of about four years, while colleges of education commonly offer the NCE, usually a three-year programme. In some countries the main route is a B.Ed or B.Sc.(Ed); in others it is a chemistry degree followed by a postgraduate teaching qualification. Programmes usually mix chemistry and education from the first year, then add teaching practice and a final project. Teaching practice is usually supervised and assessed. Master’s work adds advanced theory, research methods and a dissertation. Rules, accreditation and course titles change, so confirm the current official requirements.

sections.heading: Main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Most programmes begin with the introductory stage. You study the nature of science and chemistry; quantitative foundations; atomic structure and periodicity; chemical bonding and intermolecular forces; states of matter and solutions; organic chemistry foundations; and laboratory safety and basic techniques. Alongside these you take educational psychology for chemistry teachers and an introduction to chemistry education.

The core stage combines advanced chemistry with professional education. Chemistry topics include thermodynamics; chemical equilibrium and acid-base chemistry; chemical kinetics; electrochemistry; coordination compounds; organic reaction mechanisms; volumetric and gravimetric analysis; instrumental analysis; and environmental and green chemistry. Education topics include the chemistry curriculum and syllabus; methods of teaching chemistry; laboratory management and practical work; assessment and evaluation; educational technology; classroom management and inclusive teaching; teaching practice and professional ethics; research methods in chemistry education; and the chemistry education project.

The master’s stage adds advanced chemistry education theory; advanced research methods and dissertation; and frontiers in chemistry education. Your institution may order these differently, but the logic is usually from foundations to advanced chemistry and from observing teaching to planning, assessing and researching it.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text: Treat chemistry and education as one course, not two. For chemistry, solve problems every week, show units and significant figures, draw structures, keep a laboratory notebook and learn safety before practical work. For education, write lesson plans, explain a concept aloud and ask a peer for feedback. Use microteaching and teaching practice to test what you learn. Link each method to a theory and each theory to a classroom example. Keep a file of official curriculum documents and check current rules. For research, learn sampling, instruments, ethics and simple data analysis early. Use past questions and spaced revision. Revise little and often rather than cramming.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Common mistakes include memorising definitions without solving problems, ignoring units and significant figures, and treating safety as a formality. Some students treat education courses as easy and copy lesson plans without adapting them to learners. Others assess only recall, confuse a teaching method with subject content, or present one country’s syllabus as universal. In projects, weak samples and claims of causation from correlation are common. Not checking current regulations and not citing sources also cost marks. Read each question carefully.

keyPoints: Education Chemistry combines a chemistry major with professional teacher education.
Degree length, awards and accreditation differ by country and institution, so check your handbook.
The course moves from introductory chemistry and education to advanced chemistry, teaching methods, assessment and research.
Study by solving chemistry problems and by practising teaching with feedback.
Safety, units, significant figures and honest assessment are not optional.
In projects and assignments, check current official sources and do not present one country’s rules as universal.

en.title: Nature of Science and Chemistry
en.short: What chemistry is, how scientific knowledge is built, its branches, science versus technology, and chemistry in society.

sections.heading: What chemistry is
sections.text:
Chemistry is the study of matter: what substances are made of, how they are structured, their properties, and how they change. Matter is anything with mass and volume. A chemist may ask why a metal corrodes or how a drug acts in the body. Chemistry sits between physics, which studies matter and energy more generally, and biology, which studies living systems.

For a teacher, chemistry is not only a list of facts; it is a way of asking and testing questions about substances.

sections.heading: How knowledge is built
sections.text:
Scientific work usually begins with observation: careful noticing or measuring. From observations a scientist frames a hypothesis, a testable proposed explanation. An experiment tests it under controlled conditions, changing one variable at a time. Results may support, revise or reject the hypothesis.

A model is a simplified representation, such as a ball-and-stick drawing, used to explain or predict. A law states a consistent relationship, often in mathematical form. A theory is a broad, well-tested explanation that accounts for many observations. Theory is not a guess. The process is not a fixed ladder. A case: Amina in Kano notices nails rust faster after rain. She hypothesises that water and salt speed rusting, then compares nails in dry air, water and salt water.

sections.heading: Branches and technology
sections.text:
The main branches are organic chemistry (carbon compounds), inorganic chemistry (other elements and their compounds), physical chemistry (energy, rates and structure), analytical chemistry (identifying and measuring substances), and biochemistry (chemistry of living things). Other branches include polymer and medicinal chemistry.

Science seeks understanding; technology applies it to make tools, medicines or materials. A battery is technology; the chemistry behind it is science. The two support each other, but they are not the same.

sections.heading: Chemistry and society
sections.text: Chemistry improves life through medicines, clean water, fertilisers, fuels and materials. It also creates risks: pollution, toxic waste and accidents. Society must weigh benefits against harms. In teaching, everyday examples help students see chemistry as human work, not magic.

keyPoints: Chemistry studies matter, including its composition, structure, properties and changes.
Observation, hypothesis, experiment, model, law and theory are tools for building reliable scientific knowledge.
A law describes a consistent pattern; a theory explains why it occurs.
The main branches are organic, inorganic, physical, analytical and biochemistry.
Science seeks understanding, while technology applies scientific knowledge.
Chemistry brings benefits and risks, so society must weigh evidence and values.

en.title: Quantitative Foundations of Chemistry
en.short: SI units, uncertainty, moles, formulae, stoichiometry, solutions, graphs and logs for chemistry.

sections.heading: Units and uncertainty
sections.text: SI units are the agreed measurement system. The seven base units include the metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela. Derived units combine them, such as mol/dm³ for concentration. Every measurement has uncertainty, meaning the range within which the true value lies. Report a result with significant figures, the digits that show precision, matching the measurement, and do not round intermediate steps. In calculations, the answer should not be more precise than the least precise input.

sections.heading: Moles and formulae
sections.text: The mole is the amount containing 6.022 × 10²³ particles, the Avogadro constant. Molar mass M is the mass of one mole in g/mol. Amount n = mass ÷ M. The empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms; the molecular formula is the empirical formula multiplied by n, where n = molar mass ÷ empirical formula mass. To find an empirical formula, convert masses or percentages to moles, divide by the smallest, then adjust to whole numbers.

sections.heading: Stoichiometry and solutions
sections.text: A balanced equation gives mole ratios. The limiting reagent is used up first and sets the theoretical yield. Percentage yield = actual yield ÷ theoretical yield × 100. Concentration in mol/dm³ = amount in mol ÷ volume in dm³; convert cm³ to dm³ by dividing by 1000. Example: 4.0 g NaOH (M = 40 g/mol) is 0.10 mol. With 0.08 mol HCl, HCl is limiting, so theoretical NaCl is 0.08 mol. If 0.070 mol forms, yield = 0.070 ÷ 0.080 × 100 = 87.5%. 0.10 mol in 250 cm³ is 0.10 ÷ 0.250 = 0.40 mol/dm³.

sections.heading: Graphs, logs and data
sections.text: Rearrange formulas by doing the same operation to both sides. Plot the independent variable on the x-axis and the dependent variable on the y-axis; the slope has units and can give a constant. Logarithms turn powers into straight lines: log10(10^x) = x, and ln(e^x) = x. Handle data by tabulating values with units, calculating the mean, noting spread, and checking graphs for outliers. A graph is evidence, not decoration.

keyPoints: Convert all measurements to consistent SI units before calculating, and report answers with significant figures that match the least precise input.
Amount n = mass ÷ molar mass; one mole contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles.
Empirical formula is the simplest atom ratio; molecular formula = empirical formula × (molar mass ÷ empirical formula mass).
Use the balanced equation and the limiting reagent to find theoretical yield; percentage yield = actual ÷ theoretical × 100.
Concentration (mol/dm³) = amount (mol) ÷ volume (dm³), and 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³.
Graphs show relationships through slope and intercept; logarithms linearise power or exponential data.

en.title: Atomic Structure and Periodicity
en.short: Subatomic particles, isotopes, electron configuration, periodic table structure and trends, with teaching notes.

sections.heading: Particles and isotopes
sections.text: An atom has a nucleus of protons and neutrons, with electrons around it. Atomic number Z is the number of protons and defines the element. Mass number A is protons plus neutrons. Isotopes have the same Z but different A. Relative atomic mass Ar is the weighted mean isotope mass on the carbon-12 scale. If chlorine were 75% chlorine-35 and 25% chlorine-37, Ar = (35 × 75 + 37 × 25) ÷ 100 = (2625 + 925) ÷ 100 = 35.5. Real data differ, so use the values given.

sections.heading: Electron configuration
sections.text: Electrons occupy shells labelled by principal quantum number n. Each shell holds up to 2n² electrons and divides into subshells s, p, d and f, then orbitals. An orbital is a region where the probability of finding an electron is high; it holds at most two electrons. Fill using the aufbau principle, Pauli exclusion principle and Hund’s rule. Evidence for shells comes from line spectra and successive ionisation energies. Fine structure and small energy steps within a shell support subshells. Orbital shapes come from quantum mechanics and are supported by spectroscopy and magnetic behaviour.

sections.heading: Periodic trends
sections.text: The periodic table is ordered by increasing Z. Groups are columns with similar valence configurations; periods are rows. Atomic radius falls across a period as nuclear charge rises with little extra shielding, and rises down a group as shells are added. First ionisation energy is the energy to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms; it generally rises across and falls down. Electron affinity is the energy change when one mole of gaseous atoms gains one mole of electrons; it is usually more negative across and less negative down. Electronegativity is an atom’s tendency in a bond to attract shared electrons; it rises across and falls down.

sections.heading: Teaching the model
sections.text: In class, use spectra and ionisation-energy data to justify models, and challenge the misconception that shells are fixed orbits or that atomic radius has a sharp edge.

keyPoints: Atomic number Z is the proton count; mass number A = Z + neutrons.
Isotopes have the same Z but different A; relative atomic mass is the abundance-weighted mean on the carbon-12 scale, Ar = Σ(isotope mass × percentage abundance) ÷ 100.
Electron shells hold up to 2n² electrons and fill by the aufbau principle, Pauli exclusion principle and Hund’s rule.
Line spectra and successive ionisation energies are key evidence for shells and subshells.
Atomic radius falls across a period and rises down a group; ionisation energy, electron affinity and electronegativity generally show the opposite direction.
Periodic trends have exceptions, so use data rather than assuming a smooth change.

en.title: Chemical Bonding and Intermolecular Forces
en.short: Ionic, covalent and metallic bonding, Lewis and VSEPR shapes, polarity, intermolecular forces and properties.

sections.heading: Three main bonds
sections.text: An ionic bond forms when electrons are transferred from a metal atom to a non-metal atom, making oppositely charged ions held by electrostatic attraction. Sodium chloride is an example: Na loses one electron and Cl gains one. A covalent bond forms when atoms share a pair of electrons, as in H2 or CH4. A metallic bond forms when metal cations sit in a sea of delocalised electrons. Delocalised means the electrons are not tied to one atom.

sections.heading: Drawing and shape
sections.text: Lewis structures show valence electrons as dots or crosses. Count valence electrons, join atoms with single bonds, then add lone pairs. If two or more valid structures differ only in electron placement, they are resonance forms; the real molecule is a hybrid. Valence shell electron pair repulsion (VSEPR) theory predicts shape: electron pairs repel and stay as far apart as possible. Two pairs give linear, three trigonal planar, four tetrahedral. Lone pairs repel more, so water is bent, not linear. A bond is polar when one atom attracts the shared electrons more strongly, because it has higher electronegativity. The polarity of a molecule depends on its shape and bond dipoles. A molecule with polar bonds can be non-polar if the dipoles cancel, as in CO2.

sections.heading: Intermolecular forces
sections.text: Intermolecular forces are attractions between molecules, weaker than covalent bonds. London dispersion forces arise from temporary electron imbalance and increase with size. Dipole-dipole forces act between polar molecules. Hydrogen bonding is a strong dipole attraction when H is bonded to N, O or F and approaches a lone pair on N, O or F. It explains water’s high boiling point and ice’s low density.

sections.heading: Properties and teaching
sections.text: Bonding explains properties. Ionic solids have high melting points, conduct when molten or dissolved, and often dissolve in water. Covalent molecular substances have low melting points and usually do not conduct. Metals conduct because delocalised electrons move. A useful classroom case: ask why salt conducts in water but sugar does not. Salt gives mobile ions; sugar molecules do not. Let students build models, then explain.

keyPoints: Ionic bonds transfer electrons; covalent bonds share electrons; metallic bonds have delocalised electrons.
Lewis structures show valence electrons; resonance forms differ only in electron placement.
VSEPR counts electron pairs to predict shape; lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs.
Polarity depends on both bond dipoles and molecular shape.
Hydrogen bonding occurs when H bonded to N, O or F interacts with a lone pair on N, O or F.
Bond type and intermolecular forces explain melting point, solubility and conductivity.

en.title: States of Matter and Solutions
en.short: Kinetic theory, gas laws, phase changes, solutions, solubility and colligative properties.

sections.heading: Kinetic theory and gases
sections.text: Kinetic molecular theory explains matter as particles in constant random motion. In a gas, particles are far apart, move fast and collide elastically; pressure comes from collisions with the walls. Temperature measures average kinetic energy. The theory gives Boyle’s law (pV = constant at fixed temperature) and Charles’s law (V/T = constant at fixed pressure, with T in kelvin). Combining these with Avogadro’s law gives pV = nRT, where n is moles and R is the gas constant. At fixed T, a graph of p against 1/V is a straight line through the origin.

sections.heading: Liquids, solids and changes
sections.text: Liquids have particles close together but able to slide; solids have fixed positions and vibrate. Melting, boiling, sublimation and condensation are phase changes. At constant pressure, energy changes arrangement, not temperature, so a heating curve has flat parts. A phase diagram plots pressure against temperature and shows solid, liquid and gas regions, the triple point where all three coexist, and the critical point above which liquid and gas are indistinguishable. Impurities usually lower melting point and raise boiling point.

sections.heading: Solutions and colligative properties
sections.text: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of solute and solvent; it may be solid (an alloy), liquid (salt water) or gaseous (air). Solubility is the maximum solute that dissolves at a stated temperature. It depends on solute-solvent interactions, temperature and, for gases, pressure. Colligative properties depend on the number of dissolved particles, not their identity: vapour pressure lowering, boiling point elevation, freezing point depression and osmotic pressure. For dilute solutions, ΔTb = Kb × molality × i and ΔTf = Kf × molality × i, where molality is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent and i is the van’t Hoff factor.

sections.heading: Worked example and teaching
sections.text: Worked example: with R = 8.314 kPa dm³ mol−1 K−1, p = nRT/V = (0.50 × 8.314 × 300) ÷ 10.0 = 124.71 kPa for 0.50 mol at 300 K in 10.0 dm³. In teaching, use particle diagrams and graphs; heated particles move faster and spread further apart, the particles themselves do not expand.

keyPoints: Kinetic molecular theory treats particles as moving randomly; gas pressure arises from collisions with the walls.
Boyle’s law: pV = constant at fixed temperature; Charles’s law: V/T = constant at fixed pressure, with T in kelvin.
The ideal gas equation is pV = nRT; use consistent units for p, V, n, R and T.
Phase diagrams show solid, liquid and gas regions, the triple point and the critical point.
Solubility is the maximum solute that dissolves at a stated temperature; colligative properties depend on the number of particles.
For dilute solutions, ΔTb = Kb × molality × i and ΔTf = Kf × molality × i, with i = 1 for non-electrolytes.

en.title: Organic Chemistry Foundations
en.short: Hydrocarbons, functional groups, IUPAC naming, isomerism, homologous series and simple reactions.

sections.heading: Hydrocarbons and groups
sections.text: Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds. Carbon forms four covalent bonds and bonds to itself in chains. A hydrocarbon contains only carbon and hydrogen. Alkanes are saturated: they have only single C-C bonds and the general formula CnH2n+2. Alkenes have one C=C double bond, CnH2n. Alkynes have one triple C-C bond, CnH2n−2. A functional group is an atom or group that gives a family its characteristic reactions, such as −OH in alcohols, −COOH in carboxylic acids, C=O in aldehydes and ketones, and −NH2 in amines.

sections.heading: Naming and isomerism
sections.text: A homologous series is a family with the same functional group and similar reactions, where each member differs from the next by CH2. Boiling point usually rises as chain length increases. Isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures. For example, C4H10 has two structural isomers: butane, a straight chain, and 2-methylpropane, a branched chain. In IUPAC naming, find the longest carbon chain, number it from the end nearest a substituent, and give the substituent the lowest possible number. For 2-methylpropane the longest chain has three carbons, propane, with a methyl group on carbon 2.

sections.heading: Reactions and properties
sections.text: Simple reactions follow the functional group. Substitution: an alkane reacts with a halogen in ultraviolet light, for example methane + chlorine gives chloromethane + hydrogen chloride. Addition: an alkene adds hydrogen, bromine or water across the double bond; bromine water is decolourised, a useful test. Oxidation: a primary alcohol is oxidised first to an aldehyde, then to a carboxylic acid; ethanol can become ethanoic acid. Structure explains properties. Fuels are mostly hydrocarbons: short chains are volatile and burn easily, longer chains are less volatile. Alcohols have −OH and hydrogen bonding, so ethanol mixes with water and boils higher than the alkane of similar mass. Carboxylic acids have −COOH, donate H+ and react with bases and carbonates. For teaching, use models and local examples, ask students to name and classify, and correct the common error that isomers always have different formulas.

keyPoints: Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen; alkanes are CnH2n+2, alkenes CnH2n and alkynes CnH2n−2.
A functional group, such as −OH or −COOH, controls a family’s characteristic reactions.
A homologous series differs by CH2 and shows gradual changes in physical properties.
Isomers share a molecular formula but have different structures; C4H10 gives butane and 2-methylpropane.
Alkanes mainly undergo substitution, alkenes addition, and primary alcohols oxidation to acids.
Structure explains fuel volatility, alcohol solubility and acid reactions; teach with models and local examples.

en.title: Laboratory Safety and Basic Techniques
en.short: Hazards, risk assessment, PPE, safe disposal, common apparatus and operations, and accurate practical records.

sections.heading: Hazards and risk
sections.text: A hazard is anything that can cause harm: corrosive acids, flammable solvents, toxic salts, broken glass or hot apparatus. Risk is the chance of harm. Risk assessment means identifying hazards, deciding who may be exposed, and reducing risk before work starts. Read the safety data sheet (SDS); it gives handling and disposal advice. Use small quantities, use a fume cupboard for vapours, and know where the eyewash and fire extinguisher are. Follow local rules; they differ by country.

sections.heading: Protection and disposal
sections.text: Personal protective equipment (PPE) includes a lab coat, safety goggles, gloves and closed shoes. Choose gloves that resist the chemical. Tie back long hair and never eat or drink in the laboratory. Treat unlabelled containers as hazardous. Dispose of waste correctly: acids and bases may need neutralisation, organic solvents go into labelled solvent waste, and broken glass goes into a glass bin, not ordinary rubbish. Never pour chemicals down the sink unless local rules allow it.

sections.heading: Common operations
sections.text: Weighing uses a balance; zero it with an empty container, add the solid, and record the mass. Filtration separates a solid from a liquid using filter paper and a funnel. Crystallisation purifies a solid by dissolving it in a hot solvent, then cooling slowly so crystals form. Distillation separates liquids by boiling point. Titration finds an unknown concentration by adding a solution of known concentration from a burette until the indicator changes colour.

sections.heading: Recording and reporting
sections.text: Record what you actually did. Write observations at the time, in ink, and include units and uncertainty. For a titration, suppose 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide needs 20.0 cm³ of hydrochloric acid. Moles NaOH = 0.100 × 25.0 ÷ 1000 = 0.00250 mol. The equation is HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O, so moles HCl = 0.00250 mol. Concentration HCl = 0.00250 ÷ (20.0 ÷ 1000) = 0.125 mol/dm³. A report states aim, method, results, calculation, conclusion and errors.

keyPoints: A hazard is a source of harm; risk is the chance of harm.
Risk assessment identifies hazards and reduces exposure before work starts.
PPE includes a lab coat, goggles, suitable gloves and closed shoes.
Dispose of waste by local rules; never pour chemicals down the sink unless allowed.
Common operations include weighing, filtration, crystallisation, distillation and titration; record observations at the time.
For titration, moles = concentration × volume in dm³, and concentration = moles ÷ volume in dm³.

en.title: Educational Psychology for Chemistry Teachers
en.short: Learning theories, development, motivation, memory and misconceptions applied to chemistry teaching.

sections.heading: Learning theories
sections.text:
Behaviourism sees learning as a change in behaviour from stimulus, response and reinforcement. Clear routines, worked examples and immediate praise can shape habits.

Cognitivism treats learning as processing information: attention, encoding and retrieval. Constructivism holds that learners build new ideas on existing ones, so teachers must find out what students already believe. Ausubel called this meaningful learning. Bandura’s social learning adds modelling: a teacher who demonstrates a titration teaches method as well as content.

sections.heading: Development and memory
sections.text:
Piaget described stages from concrete to formal reasoning, though ages vary and the stages are debated. Vygotsky’s zone of proximal development is the gap between what a learner can do alone and with help; scaffolding is temporary support that closes it.

Working memory has limited capacity, so chunking and cognitive load theory matter: break a calculation into steps and remove irrelevant detail. Long-term memory grows through retrieval practice and spacing, not rereading. Transfer is using learning in a new context; near transfer is similar, far transfer is different.

sections.heading: Motivation and differences
sections.text:
Motivation may be intrinsic (interest in the task) or extrinsic (rewards, grades). Self-determination theory says autonomy, competence and relatedness support lasting motivation. Students differ in prior knowledge, pace and confidence.

Matching teaching to learning styles has weak evidence; better to vary methods and give all students practice. Chemistry misconceptions are common: that dissolving is a chemical change, that equilibrium means equal amounts, or that burning destroys matter. Diagnose them with questions, then confront them.

sections.heading: Planning and feedback
sections.text:
These ideas shape planning: start with a diagnostic question, sequence from concrete to abstract, and keep cognitive load low. Feedback should be specific, timely and focused on the task, not the person.

In one classroom example, a teacher in Kano, Nigeria, asked students to predict the mass of a reaction in an open and a closed container. Many said the mass would fall, even in the closed container. She used the disagreement to teach conservation of mass, then gave a short retrieval quiz. Formative feedback moved the class forward.

keyPoints: Behaviourism uses reinforcement; cognitivism and constructivism focus on how learners process and build ideas.
Piaget’s stages and Vygotsky’s zone of proximal development guide support, but ages vary and stage theory is debated.
Working memory is limited; chunking, cognitive load theory, retrieval practice and spacing support memory.
Motivation is stronger when autonomy, competence and relatedness are supported.
Learning styles matching has weak evidence; diagnose prior knowledge and chemistry misconceptions instead.
Feedback should be specific, timely and task-focused, and planning should start with diagnostic questions.

en.title: Introduction to Chemistry Education
en.short: Aims, history, curriculum place, teacher roles, and subject knowledge, pedagogy and professional duty.

sections.heading: Aims and history
sections.text:
Chemistry education is the field that studies how chemistry is taught and learned, and how teachers are prepared. Its aims include scientific literacy, a sound understanding of matter and change, practical and safety skills, critical thinking, and preparation for further study and work. It also aims to help citizens judge chemistry-related issues in daily life and the environment.

Chemistry has long been a school subject, but formal preparation of chemistry teachers grew with mass schooling and science curricula in the twentieth century. The details differ by country. In Nigeria, for example, B.Sc.(Ed) and B.Ed programmes combine chemistry with education courses and teaching practice. Check the current national curriculum and teacher registration rules, because they change.

sections.heading: Place in curricula
sections.text: In school curricula, chemistry usually appears in the senior secondary or upper secondary years, often after general science, and may be optional. It supports entry to medicine, pharmacy, engineering, agriculture and teaching. In teacher-education curricula, about half the work is chemistry and half is education: educational psychology, curriculum studies, methods, assessment and teaching practice. The subject courses build depth; the education courses build the ability to teach it. Programme structures vary by institution and country.

sections.heading: Teacher roles
sections.text:
A chemistry teacher plans lessons, explains ideas, runs practical work safely, assesses learning and manages the classroom. Key competencies include chemistry subject knowledge, pedagogical content knowledge, communication, laboratory safety, assessment literacy and reflective practice. Pedagogical content knowledge means knowing how to represent a topic, which misconceptions are common, and which examples and practicals help.

A small case: a teacher knows acid chemistry well, but learners call every sour liquid an acid. She uses a safe indicator demonstration and a sorting task to challenge the idea, then explains that acidity is a chemical property, not a taste. That is subject knowledge joined to pedagogy. Subject knowledge alone is not enough; pedagogy turns it into learning, and professional responsibility governs safety, fairness, honesty in assessment and respect for learners.

keyPoints: Chemistry education studies how chemistry is taught, learned and assessed, and how teachers are prepared.
Its aims include scientific literacy, practical skills, safety, critical thinking and preparation for further study and work.
School chemistry usually sits in the senior or upper secondary years and may be optional.
Teacher-education programmes combine chemistry content with education courses and teaching practice.
Chemistry teachers need subject knowledge, pedagogical content knowledge, communication, safety and assessment skills.
Professional responsibility covers safety, fairness, honesty and continuing professional development.

en.title: Physical Chemistry: Thermodynamics
en.short: Systems, the first and second laws, enthalpy, entropy, Gibbs energy and spontaneity.

sections.heading: Systems and the first law
sections.text:
A system is the part of the universe studied; the surroundings are everything else. Open systems exchange matter and energy, closed systems exchange energy only, and isolated systems exchange neither. A state function depends only on the present state, not the path. Internal energy U, enthalpy H, entropy S and Gibbs energy G are state functions; heat q and work w are path functions.

The first law is ΔU = q + w, where w is work done on the system. State whether w is work on or by the system. At constant pressure, q_p = ΔH. Calorimetry uses q = mcΔT. For 100 g water heated by 10.0 K (c = 4.18 J g−1 K−1), q = 100 × 4.18 × 10.0 = 4,180 J = 4.18 kJ.

sections.heading: Entropy and Gibbs energy
sections.text:
Entropy S measures energy dispersal. For a reversible change at temperature T, ΔS = q_rev/T. The second law says the total entropy of the universe cannot decrease: ΔS_universe = ΔS_system + ΔS_surroundings ≥ 0. At constant T and pressure, ΔS_surr = −ΔH/T, so ΔG = ΔH − TΔS decides spontaneity.

ΔG < 0 means spontaneous, ΔG = 0 equilibrium, and ΔG > 0 non-spontaneous. At a melting point ΔG = 0 and both phases coexist; below it, ΔG > 0 for melting, so solid is stable; above it, ΔG < 0, so liquid is stable. For ΔH = +50.0 kJ mol−1 and ΔS = +100 J K−1 mol−1, at 298 K TΔS = 298 × 0.100 = 29.8 kJ mol−1, so ΔG = 50.0 − 29.8 = +20.2 kJ mol−1. At 600 K, TΔS = 60.0 kJ mol−1 and ΔG = −10.0 kJ mol−1.

sections.heading: Teaching notes
sections.text: Draw the system boundary and label q and w. Use energy diagrams and ask students to test ΔG at two temperatures; this shows why ΔH alone is insufficient. Convert units first: 100 J = 0.100 kJ. State sign conventions clearly.

keyPoints: State functions depend on the state, not the path; U, H, S and G are state functions.
The first law is ΔU = q + w, with w defined as work on the system; at constant pressure q_p = ΔH.
Calorimetry uses q = mcΔT; convert units before calculating.
The second law requires ΔS_universe = ΔS_system + ΔS_surroundings ≥ 0.
At constant T and pressure, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; ΔG < 0 means spontaneous, ΔG = 0 equilibrium, ΔG > 0 non-spontaneous.
Phase stability follows ΔG: at a transition ΔG = 0, and the phase with lower G is stable.

en.title: Chemical Equilibrium and Acid-Base Chemistry
en.short: Reversible reactions, Kc and Kp, Le Chatelier, acid-base theories, pH, buffers, hydrolysis and titration curves.

sections.heading: Dynamic equilibrium
sections.text: A reversible reaction can go in both directions. At dynamic equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal, so concentrations stay constant while both reactions continue. For aA + bB <-> cC + dD, Kc = [C]^c[D]^d ÷ ([A]^a[B]^b). Kp uses partial pressures. Pure solids and liquids are omitted. The reaction quotient Q has the same form; comparing Q with K predicts the direction. Temperature changes K.

sections.heading: Le Chatelier in class
sections.text: Le Chatelier’s principle says a change in conditions shifts the equilibrium position to oppose it. Adding reactant or removing product shifts forward. Higher pressure favours fewer gas molecules. Higher temperature favours the endothermic direction, so K changes. A catalyst speeds both directions equally and does not change K. In class, ask students to predict shifts, then test a visible equilibrium, such as cobalt chloride in water and ethanol, within local safety rules.

sections.heading: Acids bases pH
sections.text: Arrhenius theory defines acids as giving H+ and bases as giving OH− in water. Brønsted-Lowry theory is broader: acid is proton donor, base is proton acceptor. Lewis theory: acid is electron-pair acceptor, base is electron-pair donor. pH = −log[H+]. At 25 °C, Kw = [H+][OH−] = 1.0 × 10^−14. For weak acid HA, Ka = [H+][A−] ÷ [HA]. Example: 0.10 M acetic acid, Ka = 1.8 × 10^−5. [H+] ≈ √(Ka × c) = √(1.8 × 10^−6) = 1.34 × 10^−3 M, so pH = −log(1.34 × 10^−3) = 2.87.

sections.heading: Buffers and titration
sections.text: A buffer is a weak acid with its conjugate base, or a weak base with its conjugate acid; it resists pH change. Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([A−] ÷ [HA]). Salt hydrolysis occurs when ions react with water; ethanoate ions, for example, make a solution basic. A titration curve plots pH against volume added. The equivalence point is the stoichiometric point; choose an indicator that changes on the steep part. At half-neutralisation of a weak acid, pH ≈ pKa.

keyPoints: At dynamic equilibrium forward and reverse rates are equal; concentrations stay constant.
Kc = [C]^c[D]^d ÷ ([A]^a[B]^b); Kp = (pC^c pD^d) ÷ (pA^a pB^b); pure solids and liquids are omitted.
Le Chatelier: concentration and pressure changes shift position; temperature changes K; a catalyst does not.
Weak acid: Ka = [H+][A−] ÷ [HA] and [H+] ≈ √(Ka × c); weak base uses Kb and [OH−] ≈ √(Kb × c).
Buffer: pH = pKa + log([A−] ÷ [HA]); titration curves guide indicator choice, and at half-neutralisation pH ≈ pKa.

en.title: Chemical Kinetics: Rates, Order and Catalysis
en.short: Covers reaction rates, rate laws, order, half-life, collision theory, Arrhenius equation, catalysis and measurement.

sections.heading: Rate and order
sections.text:
The rate of reaction is the change in concentration per unit time, mol dm−3 s−1. Average rate uses a time interval; instantaneous rate is the tangent at one time. A rate law, rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, gives the dependence on concentration.

Here k is the rate constant; m and n are the orders; overall order is m + n. Orders are found by experiment, not from the balanced equation. For a first-order reaction, t1/2 = ln 2 ÷ k ≈ 0.693 ÷ k. Example: if k = 0.020 s−1, t1/2 = 0.693 ÷ 0.020 = 34.65 s ≈ 34.7 s.

sections.heading: Collision theory and catalysis
sections.text:
Collision theory says molecules react only when they collide with enough energy and suitable orientation. Activation energy Ea is the minimum energy needed. The Arrhenius equation is k = A exp(−Ea/RT), where A is the frequency factor, R = 8.314 J mol−1 K−1 and T is in kelvin.

Taking logarithms gives ln k = ln A − Ea/(RT); a plot of ln k against 1/T has slope −Ea/R. A catalyst gives an alternative pathway with lower Ea, so more collisions succeed. It is not used up overall and may be homogeneous or heterogeneous.

sections.heading: Measuring rates
sections.text:
Rates are measured by following concentration, pressure, volume, colour or conductivity. Methods include titration after stopping the reaction, colorimetry, gas collection and mass loss. In the initial-rate method, vary one reactant at a time and compare rates to find orders.

Graphically, concentration against time gives rate from a tangent. For zero order, [A] against t is linear with slope −k; first order, ln[A] against t is linear with slope −k; second order, 1/[A] against t is linear with slope k. Half-life is read from the graph.

sections.heading: Teaching kinetics
sections.text:
Let students collect rate data and plot graphs rather than memorising formulas.

Use safe small-scale reactions to show concentration and temperature effects. Correct the common errors of confusing order with the balanced-equation coefficient and forgetting to convert temperature to kelvin.

keyPoints: Rate is concentration change per unit time; average rate uses an interval and instantaneous rate uses a tangent.
A rate law, rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, is found by experiment; overall order is m + n.
For a first-order reaction, t1/2 = ln 2 ÷ k ≈ 0.693 ÷ k, independent of initial concentration.
Collision theory requires sufficient energy and correct orientation; Ea is the minimum energy.
The Arrhenius equation is k = A exp(−Ea/RT), and ln k = ln A − Ea/(RT); the slope of ln k against 1/T is −Ea/R.
A catalyst lowers Ea by an alternative pathway; rates can be measured by titration, colorimetry, gas volume and graphical plots.

en.title: Electrochemistry
en.short: Redox, oxidation numbers, cells, electrode potentials, Nernst equation, batteries and electrolysis calculations.

sections.heading: Redox and oxidation numbers
sections.text:
Redox reactions involve electron transfer. Oxidation is loss of electrons; reduction is gain (OIL RIG). An oxidising agent accepts electrons and is reduced; a reducing agent donates electrons and is oxidised.

Oxidation numbers are bookkeeping charges. Rules: free elements are 0; monatomic ions equal their charge; oxygen is usually −2 and hydrogen +1; the sum is 0 in a neutral compound and equals the ion charge in a polyatomic ion. To balance a redox equation, split it into half-reactions, balance atoms, balance oxygen with water and hydrogen with H+, balance charge with electrons, equalise electrons, then add. In basic solution, add OH− to neutralise H+.

sections.heading: Cells and potentials
sections.text:
A galvanic (voltaic) cell has two electrodes in electrolytes, joined by a wire and a salt bridge. At the anode oxidation occurs; at the cathode reduction. The cell emf is E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode, using standard electrode potentials measured against the standard hydrogen electrode, fixed at 0 V. A positive emf means the reaction is spontaneous.

The Nernst equation corrects for non-standard concentrations: E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q, or at 298 K E = E° − (0.0592/n) log Q. Batteries are primary (not rechargeable, e.g. dry cell) or secondary (rechargeable, e.g. lead-acid, lithium-ion).

sections.heading: Electrolysis and calculations
sections.text:
Electrolysis uses electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous reaction. The anode is still oxidation and the cathode reduction. Faraday’s first law states that the mass deposited is proportional to the charge passed; the second law says that for the same charge, masses of different substances are proportional to their equivalent weights. Charge Q = I × t. Moles of electrons = Q/F, where F ≈ 96485 C/mol.

Worked example: copper from CuSO4 with 2.0 A for 30 min. Q = 2.0 × 1800 = 3600 C. Moles e− = 3600 ÷ 96485 = 0.0373 mol. Cu2+ + 2e− → Cu, so moles Cu = 0.0187 mol. Mass = 0.0187 × 63.55 = 1.19 g.

In teaching, stress that oxidation is electron loss, not always oxygen; practical cells make this concrete.

keyPoints: Oxidation is loss of electrons; reduction is gain.
Oxidation numbers track electron transfer and help balance redox equations.
Cell emf = E°cathode − E°anode; a positive value means a spontaneous reaction.
Nernst equation: E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q, or E° − (0.0592/n) log Q at 298 K.
Electrolysis uses electrical energy; charge Q = I × t and moles of electrons = Q/F.
Mass deposited in electrolysis = (M × I × t)/(n × F).

en.title: Inorganic Chemistry: Coordination Compounds
en.short: Transition metals, ligands, naming, isomerism, crystal field theory, colour, magnetism and stability.

sections.heading: Metals and ligands
sections.text: A coordination compound has a central metal ion joined to ligands. A ligand is an ion or molecule that donates a lone pair to the metal. The coordination number is the number of donor atoms bonded to the metal. Common shapes are linear (2), tetrahedral or square planar (4), and octahedral (6). Transition metals form many complexes because they have partly filled d orbitals and several stable oxidation states. For example, [Co(NH3)6]3+ is octahedral with coordination number 6.

sections.heading: Naming and isomerism
sections.text: Naming puts ligands before the metal in alphabetical order. Anionic ligands end in -o, such as chlorido and hydroxido; neutral ligands include aqua and ammine. The metal oxidation state is shown by a Roman numeral. [Co(NH3)5Cl]Cl2 is pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride. Isomerism is common. Structural isomers include ionisation and linkage isomers; stereoisomers include cis and trans forms, as in [Co(NH3)4Cl2]+. Some complexes are optically active.

sections.heading: Crystal field theory
sections.text: Crystal field theory treats metal-ligand bonds as electrostatic. In an octahedral field the five d orbitals split into a lower t2g set and a higher eg set, separated by Δo. The spectrochemical series ranks ligands by field strength, from weak I− to strong CN− and CO. Strong-field ligands give large Δo and favour low-spin filling; weak-field ligands favour high-spin. Example: in [Fe(CN)6]4−, let x be Fe oxidation state. x + 6(−1) = −4, so x = +2. Fe2+ is d6. With strong CN− it is low spin, t2g6, with no unpaired electrons.

sections.heading: Colour, magnetism, stability
sections.text: Colour appears when Δo matches visible light energy; the complex absorbs some wavelengths and transmits complementary colours. Magnetism depends on unpaired d electrons. The spin-only moment is μ = √(n(n+2)) Bohr magnetons, where n is the number of unpaired electrons; n = 4 gives √24 ≈ 4.9 BM. Stability is measured by the formation constant Kf for M + nL ⇌ MLn. Large Kf means a stable complex. Chelating ligands such as en and EDTA often increase stability through the chelate effect, an entropy effect.

keyPoints: A coordination compound has a central metal ion bonded to ligands through lone pairs; coordination number counts donor atoms.
Common geometries are linear for 2, tetrahedral or square planar for 4, and octahedral for 6.
Name ligands before the metal, use -o for anionic ligands, and give the metal oxidation state as a Roman numeral.
Crystal field theory splits d orbitals by Δo; strong-field ligands give large splitting and low-spin complexes.
Colour comes from d-d absorption of visible light, and paramagnetism from unpaired electrons, with μ = √(n(n+2)) Bohr magnetons.
Stability is measured by the formation constant Kf; chelating ligands such as EDTA often increase stability.

en.title: Organic Reaction Mechanisms: Arrows and Synthesis
en.short: Bond polarisation, curly arrows, substitution, elimination, addition, aromatic substitution and retrosynthesis.

sections.heading: Polar bonds and arrows
sections.text: A covalent bond between atoms of different electronegativity is polarised: the more electronegative atom carries partial negative charge (δ−), the other partial positive (δ+). Curly arrows show electron movement. A full arrow starts at a bond or lone pair and points to where the electron pair goes; a half arrow (fish-hook) shows one electron, as in radical reactions. The arrow never starts at an atom. Heterolytic fission gives ions; homolytic fission gives radicals.

sections.heading: Substitution and elimination
sections.text: Nucleophilic substitution replaces a leaving group with a nucleophile. SN2 is one step: the nucleophile attacks the carbon from the side opposite the leaving group, giving inversion. SN1 is two steps: the leaving group departs first, forming a carbocation, then the nucleophile attacks. Elimination removes H and leaving group to form a C=C bond. E2 is one step and needs an anti-periplanar arrangement, with the H and the leaving group in the same plane pointing opposite ways; E1 goes through a carbocation. Bulky bases and heat favour elimination; strong nucleophiles and primary halides favour SN2. Example: bromoethane + OH− gives ethanol by SN2; with hot concentrated ethanolic KOH, ethene by E2.

sections.heading: Addition and aromatic substitution
sections.text: Electrophilic addition: an alkene’s π electrons attack an electrophile, usually forming a carbocation; the nucleophile then adds. Markovnikov’s rule: in HX addition, H adds to the carbon with more H. Electrophilic aromatic substitution keeps the benzene ring. A strong electrophile, often generated by a catalyst, replaces a ring hydrogen; nitration uses HNO3/H2SO4 to give nitrobenzene. The ring’s π system is restored, which is why substitution, not addition, is favoured.

sections.heading: Interconversion and retrosynthesis
sections.text: Functional group interconversion changes one group into another, for example alcohol to alkyl halide, or aldehyde to carboxylic acid. Retrosynthesis works backwards: from target, disconnect a bond to give simpler precursors, checking that each forward step is plausible. A disconnection is not a reaction; it is a planning device. In teaching, ask students to draw every arrow, label charges, and compare substitution with elimination using the same substrate. Use models and quick diagnostic questions to expose misconceptions.

keyPoints: Curly arrows track electron pairs from source to destination; they never start at an atom.
SN2 is concerted with backside attack and inversion; SN1 proceeds via a carbocation.
E2 is concerted and anti-periplanar; E1 proceeds via a carbocation.
Addition of HX to unsymmetrical alkenes follows Markovnikov’s rule; benzene undergoes substitution to keep aromaticity.
Retrosynthesis plans routes backwards from target to precursors, using functional group interconversions.
In teaching, require arrow-by-arrow explanations and compare competing pathways on the same substrate.

en.title: Analytical Chemistry: Volumetric and Gravimetric Analysis
en.short: Sampling, errors, standard solutions, titrations, gravimetric analysis and result calculations.

sections.heading: Sampling and quality
sections.text: Analytical results are only as good as the sample. Sampling must give a representative portion of the bulk without contamination or loss. Quality control uses blanks, duplicates, certified reference materials and control charts. Errors are determinate (systematic, such as a miscalibrated balance), indeterminate (random variation) or gross (a mistake such as a misread burette). Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated results. In teaching, let learners plan sampling and explain how each error affects the result.

sections.heading: Solutions and titrations
sections.text: A standard solution has a known concentration. Prepare it from a primary standard, which is pure, stable and not hygroscopic, or standardise it against one. Concentration c = n ÷ V, with V in dm³. In acid-base titration an indicator changes colour near the equivalence point; the end point is the observed change. Redox titration uses an oxidising or reducing standard, such as potassium manganate(VII), which is self-indicating (its own colour marks the end point). Complexometric titration uses EDTA to bind metal ions; a metal-ion indicator shows the end point. Example: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 M NaOH needs 24.50 cm³ HCl. n(NaOH) = 0.100 × 25.0 ÷ 1000 = 0.00250 mol. The reaction is 1:1, so c(HCl) = 0.00250 ÷ (24.50 ÷ 1000) = 0.102 M.

sections.heading: Gravimetric and calculations
sections.text: Gravimetric analysis converts the analyte into a pure, weighable solid. The steps are precipitation, digestion (standing to form larger crystals), filtration, washing, drying or ignition, and weighing to constant mass. The precipitate must be insoluble, pure and of known formula. Calculate the analyte mass using the gravimetric factor, the ratio of the molar mass of the analyte to that of the weighed form, adjusted for the mole ratio in the balanced equation. Percentage analyte = (mass analyte ÷ mass sample) × 100. A blank and duplicate check contamination and precision. Record raw data honestly, check units (1 dm³ = 1000 cm³), and use n = cV with the balanced mole ratio. For teaching, have students plan, titrate, calculate and compare with a certified value.

keyPoints: A representative sample and quality control (blanks, duplicates, reference materials) are essential for valid results.
Determinate errors are systematic, indeterminate errors are random, and gross errors are mistakes.
A primary standard is pure, stable and not hygroscopic; standard solutions are prepared from it or standardised against it.
For titration, n = cV and c = n ÷ V, with V in dm³; the balanced equation gives the mole ratio.
Acid-base, redox and complexometric titrations use indicators or self-indicating reagents to locate the end point.
In gravimetry, percentage analyte = (mass analyte ÷ mass sample) × 100, using the gravimetric factor.

en.title: Instrumental Analysis
en.short: UV-visible and infrared spectroscopy, atomic absorption, chromatography and electroanalysis, with calibration.

sections.heading: UV-visible and IR
sections.text:
UV-visible spectroscopy measures electronic absorption. A chromophore is the absorbing group. Absorbance follows A = εcl, where ε is molar absorptivity, c concentration and l path length. It is used quantitatively for coloured or derivatised solutions.

Infrared spectroscopy measures vibrational absorption. It identifies functional groups such as O-H, C=O and N-H. The fingerprint region below about 1500 cm-1 is compared with known spectra. IR is mainly qualitative.

sections.heading: Atomic absorption
sections.text:
Atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS) measures light absorbed by free atoms in a flame or graphite furnace. A hollow cathode lamp emits the sharp line of the element measured. The sample is atomised. AAS determines metals such as lead, copper and zinc in water, soil and food.

Calibration uses standards in the same matrix. Interferences occur; check with a certified reference material or standard addition. AAS usually measures one element at a time.

sections.heading: Chromatography and electrodes
sections.text:
Chromatography separates components between a mobile phase and a stationary phase. Gas chromatography uses a gas mobile phase; liquid chromatography uses a liquid. Retention time is the time a component takes to pass through the column. Peak area is proportional to amount, so a calibration curve gives the unknown.

Simple electroanalytical methods include potentiometry, such as the pH electrode, and conductometry. A pH electrode measures potential depending on hydrogen ion activity. Ion-selective electrodes respond selectively to a particular ion. Calibrate with standard buffers or solutions.

sections.heading: Calibration and limits
sections.text:
Calibration compares instrument response with known standards. Plot response against concentration. The slope S comes from the line. The detection limit (LOD) is the smallest concentration detectable; a common convention is LOD ≈ 3s/S, where s is the standard deviation of blank measurements.

Worked example: standards of 1, 2 and 3 mg/L give absorbance 0.20, 0.40 and 0.60. Slope = 0.20 per mg/L. An unknown gives A = 0.50, so c = A/S = 0.50 ÷ 0.20 = 2.5 mg/L. Check it lies within the calibrated range.

keyPoints: UV-visible absorbance follows A = εcl, so concentration c = A/(εl) when ε and l are known.
Infrared spectra identify functional groups and are compared in the fingerprint region.
Atomic absorption uses a hollow cathode lamp and atomisation, and usually measures one element at a time.
Chromatography separates by mobile and stationary phases; retention time identifies and peak area quantifies.
Potentiometry with a pH or ion-selective electrode needs calibration with standards.
The detection limit is often estimated as LOD ≈ 3s/S, where s is the blank standard deviation and S the calibration slope.

en.title: Environmental and Green Chemistry
en.short: Air, water and soil pollution, waste treatment, green chemistry principles and teaching responsibility.

sections.heading: Pollution and chemical causes
sections.text: Pollution is the release of a substance or energy at a rate that harms living things or materials. A primary pollutant is released directly; a secondary pollutant forms in the environment, such as acid rain from sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides. Air pollution includes greenhouse gases and particulate matter. Water pollution from nitrates and phosphates in fertilisers causes eutrophication: nutrient enrichment leads to algal blooms and oxygen depletion. Heavy metals and persistent organic pollutants accumulate in soil and food chains. Soil contamination also comes from pesticides and poor waste disposal.

sections.heading: Waste treatment and recycling
sections.text: Waste treatment makes waste less harmful. Physical methods separate solids and filter water. Chemical methods neutralise acids or precipitate heavy metals as insoluble hydroxides or sulfides. Biological methods use microorganisms to break down organic matter. Recycling recovers paper, glass, metals and plastics. Solvent recovery and closed-loop processes reduce chemical waste. Sustainable chemistry designs products and processes to use less material and energy and to produce less hazardous waste.

sections.heading: Green chemistry principles
sections.text: Green chemistry designs chemical products and processes to reduce or eliminate hazardous substances. The twelve principles (Anastas and Warner, 1998) include waste prevention, atom economy, less hazardous synthesis, safer solvents, energy efficiency, renewable feedstocks and catalysis. Atom economy measures how much of the reactants ends up in the desired product: atom economy = (molar mass of desired product ÷ total molar mass of reactants) × 100%. For example, the hydration of ethene, C2H4 + H2O → C2H5OH, has reactant molar masses 28 + 18 = 46 and product molar mass 46, so atom economy = 46 ÷ 46 × 100 = 100%. A route with a by-product has lower atom economy.

sections.heading: Teaching responsibility
sections.text: Chemistry education builds environmental responsibility by linking theory to issues. Students can audit laboratory waste, measure water pH, and compare two routes by atom economy and hazard. Teachers should model safe disposal and life-cycle thinking. A project on safer solvents or battery recycling shows that chemistry is part of the solution.

keyPoints: Pollution is harm from released substances or energy; pollutants can be primary or secondary.
Air pollution from sulfur and nitrogen oxides causes acid rain; nitrates and phosphates cause eutrophication.
Waste treatment uses physical, chemical and biological methods; recycling recovers materials.
Green chemistry designs processes to prevent waste and reduce hazard.
Atom economy = (molar mass of desired product ÷ total molar mass of reactants) × 100%.
Chemistry teaching should link environmental chemistry to local practice and life-cycle thinking.

en.title: Chemistry Curriculum and Syllabus
en.short: Curriculum models, syllabus analysis, schemes of work, lesson plans and constructive alignment.

sections.heading: Curriculum models
sections.text: A curriculum is the overall plan of learning; a syllabus is the subject outline within it. Curriculum models shape chemistry teaching. Tyler’s objectives model starts from aims, states measurable objectives, selects content and evaluates. It gives clear outcomes but can narrow teaching to what is tested. Stenhouse’s process model stresses teacher judgement, inquiry and practical work. Backward design starts from the desired result and assessment evidence, then plans activities. These models influence how much practical work, local context and discovery a syllabus allows.

sections.heading: Reading the syllabus
sections.text: Analyse a syllabus before teaching it. Identify aims, topic sequence, prerequisites, depth, practical work, skills and assessment. Check whether topics build from particles and bonding to reactions and analysis. In Nigeria, for example, the senior secondary chemistry curriculum is developed nationally through NERDC, and examination bodies publish syllabuses; use the current official version. A scheme of work is the teacher’s term-by-term plan: week, topic, objectives, activities, resources and assessment. A lesson plan details one lesson: prior knowledge, introduction, development, practical or discussion, assessment and differentiation.

sections.heading: Schemes and plans
sections.text: Write objectives with observable verbs such as define, calculate, explain or design, not vague words like know. Match each objective to an activity and a check of learning. For example, Mrs Adeyemi in Ibadan plans a week on acids and bases. Her objective is that pupils explain how indicators show acidity. The activity tests local liquids with universal indicator. The assessment asks pupils to explain one result, not merely name a colour. She notes safety and resources.

sections.heading: Alignment
sections.text: Alignment, called constructive alignment, means objectives, content, activities and assessment point to the same learning. If an objective asks pupils to interpret a titration curve, a lecture on definitions is misaligned, and a recall test is misaligned. Check cognitive demand: a practical skill needs practical assessment; a reasoning aim needs a reasoning task. Review the scheme after teaching. Alignment is coherence between what you intend, what you do and what you measure.

keyPoints: A curriculum is the overall plan of learning; a syllabus is the subject outline within it.
Tyler’s objectives model, Stenhouse’s process model and backward design shape how chemistry content, practical work and assessment are planned.
Analyse a syllabus for aims, sequence, prerequisites, practical work and assessment before writing a scheme of work.
A scheme of work organises a term by week, topic, objectives, activities, resources and assessment; a lesson plan details one lesson.
Constructive alignment means objectives, activities and assessment all target the same learning at the same cognitive demand.
Use the current official syllabus for your country, because curriculum bodies and examination boards revise requirements.

en.title: Methods of Teaching Chemistry
en.short: Pedagogical content knowledge, teaching methods, activity sequencing, lesson planning and evaluation in chemistry.

sections.heading: What PCK means
sections.text: Pedagogical content knowledge (PCK) is the teacher’s special knowledge of how to make a subject learnable. It joins deep chemistry with knowledge of common misconceptions, useful examples, representations and the questions students ask. A teacher with PCK knows why the mole is hard, which particle diagrams help, and when an analogy misleads. It grows from subject study, lesson planning, classroom observation and reflection.

sections.heading: Choosing methods
sections.text: Inquiry asks students to investigate a question and explain evidence, while guided inquiry gives more structure. Demonstration shows a process or hazard safely while the teacher narrates thinking. Discussion develops explanation through talk. Problem-solving teaches a strategy, such as identifying knowns, choosing a relationship and checking units. Projects run over time and end in a product or report. Match the method to the objective: a quick particle idea may suit demonstration, while a reversible-reaction misconception may need discussion. Sequence from concrete to abstract, and revisit hard ideas in new contexts.

sections.heading: Planning a lesson
sections.text: A chemistry lesson plan states measurable objectives, prior knowledge, materials, sequence, timing and assessment. Write objectives as observable actions: students will balance three equations, or explain electrolysis using particle diagrams. Begin with a short recall check, then introduce the idea, model it, give guided practice and finish with independent work. For difficult concepts, use a concrete example first. In a case, Mr Adeyemi in Ibadan teaches ionic bonding: students first arrange ions on cards, then draw dot-and-cross diagrams, then explain why sodium chloride conducts when molten. He plans a demonstration, pair discussion and a short exit task.

sections.heading: Evaluating learning
sections.text: Evaluation asks whether the lesson worked. Check the exit task against the objective, note misconceptions, and ask whether the method helped or hindered. Use a simple tally: if 18 of 30 students balance the equation correctly, the success rate is 18 ÷ 30 = 60 per cent. Follow up with targeted practice. Ask students for one-minute feedback, and record what you will change next time. Evaluation closes the planning cycle.

keyPoints: Pedagogical content knowledge combines chemistry understanding with ways to make it learnable.
Inquiry, demonstration, discussion, problem-solving and project work serve different objectives.
Match method to objective and sequence activities from concrete to abstract.
A lesson plan states measurable objectives, prior knowledge, materials, sequence, timing and assessment.
Evaluation compares evidence of learning with the objective and records changes.
If 18 of 30 students succeed, the success rate is 18 ÷ 30 = 60 per cent.

en.title: Laboratory Management and Practical Work
en.short: Running a school chemistry laboratory safely, teaching practical lessons and assessing practical work.

sections.heading: Organising the laboratory
sections.text:
A school chemistry laboratory is a teaching space and a store of hazards. Management means clear responsibility, an inventory, locked storage, ventilation, an eyewash and a spill kit. Store chemicals by compatibility: acids apart from bases, oxidisers away from flammable liquids. Keep safety data sheets (SDS) accessible. Label each container with name, concentration, date and hazard. Prepare reagents with glassware and distilled water.

Worked example: to make 250 cm³ of 0.10 mol/dm³ sodium chloride from 1.0 mol/dm³ stock, use C1V1 = C2V2. V1 = (0.10 × 250) ÷ 1.0 = 25 cm³. Measure 25 cm³ stock into a 250 cm³ volumetric flask, make up to the mark. Check: 0.025 mol in 0.250 dm³ = 0.10 mol/dm³. Label it.

sections.heading: Risk assessment and first aid
sections.text:
Risk assessment identifies hazards, who may be harmed, controls and review. Hazards include chemicals, glass, heat, electricity and behaviour. Use the hierarchy of control: eliminate or substitute first, then engineering controls, safe procedures, and personal protective equipment last. Check local regulations and school policy; they vary by country.

For first aid, know emergency numbers, the trained first-aider, eyewash and spill kit. Follow SDS and local first-aid guidance; do not improvise treatments. Record incidents and near misses.

sections.heading: Designing practical lessons
sections.text: A practical lesson needs a clear learning aim, not just activity. Choose a demonstration or a student practical by weighing risk, time and equipment. The pre-lab stage gives the purpose, safety points, procedure and a data table. Use a predict, observe, explain cycle so students connect observations to chemistry ideas. Plan group roles and inclusive access, and rehearse the practical before the lesson.

sections.heading: Assessing practical work
sections.text: Assess practical skills and reports separately. For skills, use a checklist or rubric with criteria such as setting up, technique, safety, observation and teamwork. For reports, check data recording, calculations, graphs, interpretation and discussion of error. Mark to shared criteria and give feedback that students can act on. Practical assessment is stronger when it is planned with the lesson, not added at the end.

keyPoints: Store chemicals by compatibility and keep safety data sheets accessible.
Label reagents with name, concentration, date and hazard.
For dilution, C1V1 = C2V2; check that the final concentration is sensible.
Risk assessment identifies hazards, controls and review, and first aid follows local guidance and SDS.
Practical lessons need a clear learning aim, pre-lab safety and a predict, observe, explain cycle.
Assess practical skills with a rubric and reports for data, calculations, interpretation and error.

en.title: Assessment and Evaluation in Chemistry
en.short: Formative and summative assessment, chemistry objectives and items, marking, validity, practicals and feedback.

sections.heading: Formative and summative
sections.text: Assessment is the systematic gathering of evidence about learning; evaluation is the judgement made from that evidence, including about a course. Formative assessment happens during teaching and is low stakes. It gives feedback and helps the teacher adjust. A quick exit ticket asking students to balance one equation, or to explain why a salt solution conducts electricity, is formative. Summative assessment comes at the end of a unit or course and is graded, for example a terminal chemistry examination. It certifies achievement. Both are needed: formative assessment guides learning, summative assessment reports it.

sections.heading: Objectives and items
sections.text: Write objectives that name observable chemistry actions: balance an equation, calculate moles from mass, explain a trend, or handle a burette safely. A table of specifications, or test blueprint, maps objectives to items and cognitive levels so the test samples the syllabus fairly. Items must use correct symbols, units and equations. Avoid vague verbs such as know or understand. For a calculation item, check the answer yourself. Example: moles of NaOH in 4.0 g, molar mass 40 g/mol, are 4.0 ÷ 40 = 0.10 mol.

sections.heading: Marking and quality
sections.text: Marking should follow a written scheme that awards method marks as well as final answers. Feedback should be specific, timely and actionable: say what was wrong and what to do next. Validity means the assessment measures the intended learning, not unrelated reading difficulty. Reliability means consistent results across markers and occasions. Clear criteria, moderation and enough items improve reliability. Item analysis helps. Difficulty p is the number correct divided by the number attempting, so a high p means an easy item. If 18 of 30 students answer correctly, p = 18 ÷ 30 = 0.60.

sections.heading: Practicals and improvement
sections.text: Practical assessment should judge planning, technique, safety, observations, calculations and reporting. Use a rubric or checklist with clear descriptors, and assess the process as well as the written report. Results should close the teaching loop: analyse item and practical errors, reteach weak topics, and revise schemes of work. Keep records and discuss patterns with colleagues. Assessment then improves teaching rather than only ranking students.

keyPoints: Formative assessment is low stakes and during teaching; summative assessment is graded and at the end.
Objectives should use observable verbs and match the chemistry content and cognitive level.
A table of specifications helps a test sample the syllabus fairly.
Validity is measuring the intended learning; reliability is consistency across markers and occasions.
Item difficulty p = number correct ÷ number attempting; 18 ÷ 30 = 0.60.
Practical work needs clear rubrics, and results should be used to reteach and improve teaching.

en.title: Educational Technology in Chemistry
en.short: Selecting, checking and planning models, videos, simulations, virtual labs and mobile resources for chemistry lessons.

sections.heading: Tools and their roles
sections.text: Educational technology is the planned use of tools and resources to support learning. A model is a simplified representation of an object or idea, such as a ball-and-stick model of a molecule. A chart is a visual display of information, such as a flow diagram or graph. A video can show a process that is too slow, fast, costly or dangerous to repeat live. A simulation is an interactive program that lets learners change variables and observe results. A virtual laboratory simulates apparatus and measurements. Mobile resources include apps, e-books and short videos used on phones or tablets.

sections.heading: Checking digital tools
sections.text: Judge a tool first by accuracy. Check the author or publisher, the date, the source of any data, and whether the chemistry matches the syllabus and current conventions. Look for errors in labels, units and equations. Then judge accessibility: captions for video, readable text, screen-reader support, low-bandwidth or offline versions, language, cost and device needs. A tool that excludes some students is not neutral. Prefer tools you can test yourself and that allow prediction, discussion and feedback, not passive watching.

sections.heading: Planning a lesson
sections.text: Start with the learning objective, then choose technology only if it helps that objective. Plan the activity around the tool: what students do before, during and after. Test the equipment and network in advance, prepare a non-digital backup, and check privacy and safety. For example, Mr Adeyemi has one projector and some student phones. He checks an animation of particle motion for accuracy, adds captions, prints a diagram as backup, and asks pairs to predict before showing it. He assesses learning with a short explanation, not the animation itself.

sections.heading: Models and limits
sections.text: Models and virtual laboratories are not replacements for real practical work where hands-on skills and safety are the aim. Use them to prepare, rehearse, visualise or extend, and state their limits. Physical models can be touched; digital models can show invisible processes.

keyPoints: Educational technology is the planned use of tools to meet a learning objective.
Choose models, charts, videos, simulations, virtual labs or mobile resources for what they add, not for novelty.
Check digital tools for chemical accuracy, source, date, labels and units.
Check accessibility: captions, readable text, offline or low-bandwidth use, language, cost and device needs.
Plan the student activity around the tool and prepare a non-digital backup.
Virtual labs support practice but do not replace hands-on work where safety and manipulative skills are the aim.

en.title: Classroom Management and Inclusive Teaching in Chemistry
en.short: Safe chemistry routines, group work, behaviour, mixed abilities, disability, language and anxiety.

sections.heading: Safe routines and supervision
sections.text: Classroom management means the planned routines and responses that keep a class safe, orderly and learning. In chemistry, the laboratory adds hazards, so management includes risk assessment, clear entry and exit routines, supervision, and stopping work when rules are broken. Follow your school and country safety rules. A teacher should know the emergency plan, keep records, and never leave a practical class unsupervised. Safety is not a separate topic here; it is the first condition for teaching.

sections.heading: Behaviour and group work
sections.text: Behaviour management works best when expectations are taught, not only punished. State a few rules, rehearse routines, and use calm, private correction. Group work can improve understanding if roles are clear: recorder, materials manager, safety monitor, reporter. Groups need a task with a shared product, and the teacher moves around to check understanding and safety. Avoid letting one learner do all the work.

sections.heading: Inclusive teaching
sections.text: Inclusive teaching adapts the same learning goal to different learners. Mixed ability classes need varied support, such as worked examples, structured questions and extension tasks. Gender should not limit participation; invite all learners to handle apparatus and lead groups. Disability may require reasonable accommodation, meaning a fair change to how learning is accessed, such as enlarged print, a seated laboratory place, extra time or an assistant. Language needs call for clear speech, key word lists, diagrams and allowing learners to explain ideas in a first language before English. Do not lower chemistry standards; remove barriers.

sections.heading: Anxiety and a case
sections.text: Chemistry anxiety is fear or tension about chemistry tasks, often from past failure or fear of chemicals. Reduce it with small steps, predictable routines, worked examples and chances to practise without public shame. Case: in a mixed class, Mr Okafor pairs a confident learner with a shy learner for a titration planning task. He gives a key word list, a role card and a simpler calculation step. He checks both students’ plans and praises effort. The goal remains the same; support differs.

keyPoints: Classroom management in chemistry combines clear routines with active laboratory supervision and local safety rules.
Behaviour is managed best by teaching expectations and correcting calmly and privately.
Group work needs assigned roles and a shared product so all learners contribute.
Inclusive teaching keeps the chemistry goal and changes access, using varied support, gender-fair participation, accommodations and language help.
Reasonable accommodation is a fair change to how a learner accesses learning, not a lower standard.
Chemistry anxiety falls with small steps, predictable routines, worked examples and low-risk practice.

en.title: Teaching Practice and Professional Ethics
en.short: School placement roles, observation, lesson planning, reflection, ethics and teacher regulation.

sections.heading: Placement roles
sections.text: A teaching practice placement places a trainee in a school under a mentor or cooperating teacher, a university supervisor and the school head. The trainee must be punctual, follow school policies, safeguard learners, keep records and report concerns. The mentor guides planning and gives feedback; the supervisor checks professional progress. In Nigeria the Teachers Registration Council of Nigeria (TRCN) is the statutory regulator for teachers. Other countries have their own bodies, such as the Department for Education in England, which regulates teacher conduct. Requirements change, so check the current official source.

sections.heading: Observe, plan, teach
sections.text: Observation means watching a lesson with a focus, such as questioning, board work, practical demonstrations or safety, and recording evidence. Lesson planning states objectives, prior knowledge, materials, activities, assessment and timing. For chemistry, include a risk assessment for practical work. Teaching then uses clear explanation, demonstration, questioning and feedback. After the lesson, reflect: what worked, what evidence shows learning, and what to change. A concrete case: Ngozi, a trainee in Kaduna, planned a titration lesson but ran out of time. Her mentor noted that she spent too long explaining and too little time on guided practice. Her next plan shortened the explanation and added a timed pair task.

sections.heading: Professional ethics
sections.text: Professional ethics are the standards expected of a teacher. Confidentiality means keeping learner records, marks and family information private, sharing only with those who need it. Fairness means treating learners equally, avoiding favouritism and bias, and making reasonable adjustments for inclusive learning. Relationships with learners need professional boundaries: no exploitation, no romantic involvement and no private contact that could harm or be misunderstood. With colleagues, be respectful and collaborative. With parents, communicate honestly and protect privacy. Follow the school’s child protection and reporting procedures.

keyPoints: Teaching practice is a supervised school placement with a mentor, university supervisor and school head.
Observation should have a focus and be recorded as evidence.
A lesson plan states objectives, activities, assessment, timing and, for chemistry, practical risk assessment.
Reflection uses evidence from the lesson to improve the next plan.
Confidentiality, fairness and professional boundaries are core teacher ethics.
In Nigeria the TRCN regulates teachers; other countries have their own bodies, so check current requirements.

en.title: Research Methods in Chemistry Education
en.short: Framing questions, designs, sampling, instruments, ethics, data analysis and report writing.
